unit.title: Collecting Data
unit.blurb: Planning a statistical investigation: types of data, questionnaires, data-collection sheets, populations and samples.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Plan an investigation: choose the data to collect, classify data, and design questionnaires and data-collection sheets.

O2.t: Understand populations and samples, choose a sample size and recognise how sampling can introduce bias.

lesson.t: Is the canteen food healthy enough?
p: The student council wants to know: **Do students eat enough fruit and vegetables at lunch, and does it differ between year groups?**
What data would you collect, from whom, and how? Think about it before you read on.

lesson.t: How do I plan data collection?
p: Step 1: Split the main question into linked questions.
Step 2: For each, decide the data, its type, and primary or secondary source.
Step 3: Choose the method: questionnaire, observation, experiment or records.
Step 4: Design clear, unbiased questions with complete, non-overlapping options; pilot them.

captions: The student council wants to know two things.
Do students eat enough fruit and vegetables at lunch?
And is it different in different year groups?
Which data would help to answer the question?
Pause the video and choose.
We need two things for each student: how many portions they eat, and their year group.
The canteen menu alone would not tell us what students actually eat.
Remember the types of data.
Categorical data is words, like a favourite fruit.
Discrete data is counted, like the number of portions.
Continuous data is measured, like a mass.
A big question usually splits into smaller linked questions.
Each one needs its own data.
Data you collect yourself is primary data.
Data that someone else has already collected, like a website or a report, is secondary data.
Your turn.
Data that you collect yourself is called what?
Pause the video and choose.
Data you collect yourself is primary data.
Rainfall over 30 years, from a weather service, is secondary data.
A good question is clear, and it is not personal.
It must not be leading.
A leading question pushes people towards an answer, like: don't you agree that vegetables are boring?
Response boxes must cover every possible answer, without overlapping.
Here is the method.
Step 1: split the main question into linked questions.
Step 2: for each one, decide the data, its type, and whether it is primary or secondary.
Step 3: choose a method: a questionnaire, an observation, an experiment or a search of records.
Step 4: test your questionnaire on a few people first.
This is called a pilot.
Improve this question: most people think our library is too small.
Do you agree?
It is leading, because it tells you what other people think.
A better question is neutral, with boxes for every view.
Here is another question: do you eat a lot of fruit?
Your turn.
What is the problem with this question?
Pause and choose.
A lot is vague.
It means different things to different people.
Ask for a number, over a fixed time: how many portions of fruit did you eat yesterday?
Plates have between 0 and about 300 grams of food waste.
Choose groups for the mass, m.
Use equal widths with no gaps and no overlaps: 0 is less than or equal to m, which is less than 50.
Then 50 to 100, and so on, up to 300.
That makes 6 groups.
Leo writes response boxes for the question: how old are you?
Which line goes wrong first?
Line 1 is wrong.
A 12 year old could tick two boxes, and a 17 year old has no box to tick.
Better boxes do not overlap, and cover everyone.
Many countries run a census about every 10 years.
Every household answers the same questions, about who lives there and how they live.
Before the real census, officials test the questions on a small group first, to find confusing questions.
That is a pilot, just like the one in step 4.
One last question.
Testing a questionnaire on a few people first is called what?
Pause the video and choose.
It is called a pilot.
It helps you fix unclear questions and missing boxes before the real survey.
To remember: break a big question into linked questions.
Decide the type of data, and whether it is primary or secondary.
Questions must be clear, and not leading.
Response boxes must cover every answer, with no overlaps.
And pilot your questionnaire first.

p: A school has **1200 students**. The council has one week to find out what students think of the canteen.
Should they ask everyone? If not, how many, and how should they choose them? Think about it before you read on.
The population is everyone you are interested in; a sample is the group you actually ask.

qq.prompt: For the canteen question, the population is …

head: Method
How
Strength
Weakness
rows: every member has an equal chance (random numbers)
every k-th person on a list (e.g. every 20th)
a pattern in the list can cause bias
sample each group in proportion (e.g. by year)

p2: For 1200 students, a random or stratified sample of about 100 (≈ 8%) is sensible.

p: A sample is **biased** if some groups are more likely to be included than others – e.g. asking only students in the lunch queue misses those who bring packed lunches.
A **larger** sample usually gives more reliable results, but takes more time and money. Too small (e.g. 10) can easily mislead.

qq.prompt: Choosing every 12th name from the register is …

lesson.t: How do I choose a good sample?
p: Step 1: Define the population clearly.
Step 2: Choose a sample size that balances reliability with time and cost.
Step 3: Choose a method that gives every member a fair chance (random, systematic or stratified).
Step 4: Check for bias: who might be left out?

captions: A school has 1,200 students.
The council has one week to find out what students think of the canteen.
Should they ask every student?
Is asking all 1,200 students in one week a good plan?
Pause the video and choose.
It is possible, but very slow.
It is more practical to ask a smaller group, called a sample.
The question is how to choose it fairly.
Remember: the population is everyone you are interested in.
Here it is all 1,200 students.
The sample is the group you actually ask.
In a simple random sample, every member has an equal chance of being chosen, for example using random numbers.
In a systematic sample, you choose every k-th name on a list, like every 12th name.
In a stratified sample, each group, like each year group, is included in proportion to its size.
A convenience sample just asks whoever is easy to ask, like your friends.
It is quick, but it is often biased.
Your turn.
Asking your friends is which kind of sampling?
Pause the video and choose.
Asking your friends is convenience sampling.
Your friends may think alike, so the results may not represent everyone.
A sample is biased if some groups are more likely to be included than others.
Asking only students in the lunch queue misses everyone who brings a packed lunch.
A larger sample usually gives more reliable results, but it takes more time and costs more.
Here is the method.
Step 1: define the population clearly.
Step 2: choose a sample size that balances reliability with time and cost.
Step 3: choose a method that gives everyone a fair chance: random, systematic or stratified.
Step 4: check for bias.
Ask yourself: who might be left out?
Years 7, 8 and 9 have 400, 500 and 300 students.
Take a stratified sample of 60.
60 out of 1,200 is 1 in 20.
So divide each year by 20.
400 divided by 20 is 20.
500 divided by 20 is 25.
300 divided by 20 is 15.
Check: 20 plus 25 plus 15 is 60.
Your turn.
Take a stratified sample of 30 from 200 boys and 100 girls.
How many boys?
Pause and work it out.
There are 300 students.
30 out of 300 is 1 in 10.
200 divided by 10 is 20 boys, and 100 divided by 10 is 10 girls.
Choose a systematic sample of 50 from a list of 1,200 names.
1,200 divided by 50 is 24, so choose every 24th name.
Pick a random starting point between 1 and 24, say 7.
Then take names 7, 31, 55, and so on.
To find out how much exercise adults do, a student asks people leaving a gym.
What is wrong?
Gym users exercise more than most people, and people who never exercise are missed.
The sample is biased, and the results will be too high.
Amir wants to find the favourite sport of students in his school.
Here is his plan.
Which line is wrong?
Line 2 is wrong.
Football club members are much more likely to choose football.
The sample is biased.
A fairer plan is a random or stratified sample from the whole school register.
Before an election, polling companies ask about 1,000 to 2,000 people, not millions.
They choose them carefully, so that ages, regions and other groups are in proportion.
A well-chosen sample can be surprisingly accurate.
A badly chosen one, even a huge one, can be very wrong.
One last question.
Is a sample of 8 students likely to be reliable?
Pause the video and choose.
A sample of 8 is too small.
It is likely to be unreliable, because a few unusual answers change the results a lot.
To remember: samples can be random, systematic, stratified or convenience.
In a stratified sample, each group is in proportion.
A biased sample leaves groups out.
Bigger samples are more reliable, but they cost more time.
